paper_title: Duopra: From Full-Duplex Conversation to Full-Duplex Agency

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Full-duplex interaction models exhibit strong conversational agency, enabling natural, low-latency turn-taking, backchannels, and interruptions. However, completing tasks further requires task agency: timely tool invocation and argument revision following user corrections. Frontend-backend agents separate initiation from execution: the frontend decides whether and what to request, while the backend determines how. Execution can be offloaded, but unsent requests cannot be executed, and incomplete ones can misdirect the backend. On Full-Duplex-Bench v3 (FDB v3), most failures of Realtime-Venus-Audio + Harness in our streaming pipeline occur before a domain tool executes. We introduce Duopra, a full-duplex interaction model that learns task execution alongside conversational control. Duopra treats the backend as a tool, accepting a self-contained natural-language request. Direct calls and backend delegation share an action interface and requirements for faithful initiation and correct execution. Its three-stage training combines protocol SFT, full-duplex RL rewarding timely and complete execution, and projector-only repair of talker conditioning after thinker updates. With the same backend, Pass@1 rises from 4.7% to 44.7%; Duopra achieves 47.7% calling tools directly (26.0% after SFT) and 49.3% with a DeepSeek backend. It improves three FDB v1.0 takeover rates over the base model. These results show that task agency can coexist with key conversational agency.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Full-duplex interaction models handle pauses, backchannels, turn-taking and interruptions, exhibiting conversational agency: deciding when * Equal contribution. Work done during Chiyu Chens internship at Tencent. Project lead. Corresponding authors. 1 to listen, speak, stop or resume (Défossez et al., 2024; Cui et al., 2026; Lin et al., 2025a, 2026c). Tool use adds task agency: deciding when to act, preserving the users latest intent and completing the requested steps (Yao et al., 2025a; Lin et al., 2026a). Full-duplex agency requires coordinating these decisions as speech and execution results arrive. Frontendbackend agents address task agency through conversational frontend that sends natural-language requests to tool-using backend (Venus Team (Ant Group), Tsinghua University, 2026; Huang et al., 2026; Hu et al., 2026). We ask: What limits task success in frontend backend agents, and how can full-duplex interaction model acquire reliable task agency? In this architecture, the frontend must still turn an evolving request into an executable task. It must determine whether information is sufficient, incorporate corrections, and initiate request that preserves the required values and steps. Failures at this stage can prevent an otherwise capable backend from acting. When tool schemas are available only to the backend, the frontend must also convey the request without direct access to the tools argument requirements, potentially introducing additional clarification and execution delays. Figure 1 illustrates these demands with real scenario from Full-Duplex-Bench v3 (FDB v3; Lin et al., 2026a): the user changes both the product and quantity, while adding the item requires result from the preceding search. We investigate this issue on FDB v3. In our streaming pipeline, Realtime-Venus-Audio (RVAudio) with its Harness, denoted RV-Audio + Harness, hands off requests to the backend in 11.0% of sessions and passes 4.7%. Holding those hand-offs fixed caps success at this 11.0% handoff ceiling, even with perfect backend execution (Section 5.3). The result identifies limited initiation in this configuration, rather than general Figure 1: Frontend responsibility in an evolving FDB v3 request (ecommerce_19; schematic). Execution can be offloaded, but initiating faithful request remains frontend responsibility. The user corrects both the product (laptop to tablet) and the quantity (two to one); add_to_cart depends on the product ID returned by search_products. (a) When domain schemas are available only to the backend, the frontend may need successive hand-offs to convey the evolving request, making it harder to preserve corrections and tool dependencies. (b) With schemas visible, Duopra can issue the corrected domain-tool calls directly without hand-off, while query(task) remains available. Crossed-out values and curved arrows denote superseded requests. Table 16(a) reports an observed delegated success on this request. limit on delegation. The frontend therefore needs task agency: execution can be offloaded, but initiating faithful request remains frontend responsibility. Learning this competence requires coordinating conversation with execution: the frontend must act when information is sufficient, incorporate corrections, and complete dependent steps. Moreover, updating the language model (the thinker) can alter the hidden states that condition the speech generator (the talker) and degrade intelligibility. We introduce Duopra, full-duplex interaction model built on RV-Audio that controls conversation and emits private tool actions. It represents the backend as query(task), tool with self-contained natural-language argument, so direct calls and delegation share an action interface and execution criteria. Its training proceeds in three stages: protocol supervised fine-tuning (SFT) teaches schema-based calling and clarification; full-duplex reinforcement learning (RL) rewards timely, complete and grounded execution; and projector-only repair realigns talker conditioning after thinker updates. Duopra improves task completion through both direct execution and backend delegation; with the same Qwen3-8B backend, it raises Pass@1 from 4.7% to 44.7%. Its takeover rates for turn-taking, pauses and interruptions on FDB v1.0 (Lin et al., 2025a) all improve over the base model, showing that task learning can coexist with turn-taking control, although spontaneous backchanneling is not retained. Our main contributions are: 1. We formalize full-duplex agency as joint conversational and task decisions, and analyze frontend initiation, argument fidelity and task completion. 2. We introduce Duopra, full-duplex interaction model that learns direct tool use and represents backend delegation as naturallanguage-argument tool in the same action interface. 3. We develop three-stage procedure combining protocol SFT, execution-based fullduplex RL and projector-only repair, and evaluate task gains together with conversational and speech changes.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Full-duplex interaction systems. Full-duplex models listen while speaking, requiring continu2 ous decisions about when to respond, yield or remain silent (Skantze, 2021). dGSLM models textless two-channel dialogue (Nguyen et al., 2023), while Moshi adds an inner text monologue to parallel audio streams (Défossez et al., 2024) and SyncLLM synchronizes generation with realworld clock (Veluri et al., 2024). Other systems adapt pretrained LLMs to duplex speech (Wang et al., 2025; Hu et al., 2025; Yu et al., 2025b; Yao et al., 2025b; Chen et al., 2025; Fang et al., 2026; Cui et al., 2026). The FDB series evaluates pauses, backchannels, turn-taking, interruptions, overlap and multi-turn dialogue (Lin et al., 2025a, 2026c,b), with v3 extending evaluation to tool use on real, disfluent speech (Lin et al., 2026a). Frontendbackend agents. Delegation separates ongoing conversation from asynchronous task execution. Realtime-Venus executes each <delegate> request in its asynchronous Harness runtime (Venus Team (Ant Group), Tsinghua University, 2026), JoyAI-VL-Interaction chooses every second among speaking, silence and delegation (Yao et al., 2026), and DuplexOmni connects the frontend to pluggable thinking layer (Huang et al., 2026). Hu et al. (2026) train speech frontend to emit delegation token and forward streaming ASR transcripts to text backend. SALMONN-duo learns when to answer directly or invoke an asynchronous backend, using cost-aware RL to balance performance and backend use (Yu et al., 2026), while DuplexAgent-RSI improves the delegation harness from interaction traces (Shen et al., 2026). Task success in this setting depends on both the frontends requests and the backends execution. Direct tool use and hybrid routing. Speech frontends can call tools directly, extending their role beyond conversation and delegation. GPTRealtime supports asynchronous function calling (OpenAI, 2025); NemotronLabs VoiceChat and Qwen-Audio-3.1-Realtime also support agentic voice interaction (Balam et al., 2026; Bao et al., 2026). DuplexSLA coordinates speech, language and action (Zhang et al., 2026), while SHANKS initiates tool calls during user speech (Chiang et al., 2026). Qwen-Audio-Agent provides harness supporting direct tool calls and spawn_thinking delegation (Deng et al., 2026). Duopra studies how the full-duplex frontend learns to initiate faithful execution, through either native calls or delegation, and analyzes the resulting task failures. Post-training for spoken agents. Speech posttraining targets semantic quality through user interactions and AI feedback (Wu et al., 2025a; Lin et al., 2025b), and conversational behavior through preference optimization (Fang et al., 2026) and RL (Ohashi et al., 2026; Hsiao et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026). Qwen-Audio-3.1-Realtime uses GRPO for tool use and aligns whether and when to speak or act (Bao et al., 2026). Duopra trains task execution using time-anchored deadlines and outcome tiers. It then updates only the thinkertalker projector to address speech degradation, with regularization toward its original weights (Li et al., 2018). Appendix reviews broader work on tool learning, spoken evaluation, asynchronous execution and information sufficiency.

sections.title: 3 Full-Duplex Agency
sections.content: Section 1 asks what limits task success in frontendbackend agents and how full-duplex interaction model can acquire reliable task agency. To make this question precise, we model the frontend as one streaming policy whose actions depend on the tools it can call. Backend delegation and direct tool calling then become settings of one model, and information sufficiency and task success are defined independently of which component executes call. One policy for speech and action. User audio arrives in units x1, x2, . . . of length . At unit t, the frontend reads xt and the observations et injected by then, which hold the schemas of the tools it can call and the results of its earlier calls, and emits yt = (mt, wt, at): turn state mt {listen, speak}, text tokens wt, which are voiced, and possibly empty private action at, which is never voiced. The policy is causal: πθ (yt xt, et, y<t) . (1) Conversational agency decides mt and wt: when to listen, speak, stop or resume through pauses, backchannels and interruptions. Task agency decides at, which tool to call with which arguments, and the part of wt that serves the request: asking for missing value and reporting what call returned. Full-duplex agency is making both decisions well in one causal policy. Tools and exposures. Each domain tool has JSON schema with required and optional arguments, and the backend agent is one more tool, query(task), whose argument is self-contained natural-language task that executes with its own tools FB (Appendix C). The frontend calls tool from its set {query} through one action, call(f, args); an auxiliary select action retrieves further schemas in . Request-based delegation, through which frontendbackend agents such as Realtime-Venus hand the backend request, exposes only the backend (T = {query}, with the domain tools in FB); direct calling exposes the domain tools (T = F); and their union exposes both. We call these three tool exposures Backend, Direct and Both. Under Both, the model chooses the route through this interface, without separate dispatcher; execution is checked against the same required domain calls (Section 5.3). Information sufficiency. call is justified only if each of its required arguments has source: the users speech, in which the last correction is final (in Figure 1, one tablet rather than two laptops); the result of an earlier call; or the session context with the defaults it specifies. If required value has no source, the frontend should ask for the missing items only and act once they are given; missing optional arguments take their defaults. The criterion is the same for both routes. delegated task must preserve the latest known values and required steps, while identifying any values to be supplied by earlier tool results. The frontend uses the backend descriptions actually exposed in its context (Appendix C). Success criteria. Each request has gold calls C, possibly dependent on earlier results or conditions. Task success requires (i) calls: the calls executed by the frontend or backend match C, with all normalized arguments correct and no call missing or extra; (ii) grounding: the spoken answer rests only on returned observations and covers the request; and (iii) timeliness: if information is sufficient, the frontend acts within kact units after the request ends, and otherwise asks only for missing items. Conversational control requires (iv) that the frontend take the turn when the user finishes but not in pauses, stop within kstop units of an interruptions onset, and continue through backchannels and background speech. Initiation, execution and control. On FDB v3, every session holds one request that needs at least one call. Under request-based delegation, domain tool runs only after the frontend calls query, so Pass@1 factors into the share of sessions with such hand-off, which the frontend alone decides, and the pass rate of these sessions, which depends on both the task the frontend writes and the backend that executes it. However strong the backend, Pass@1 cannot exceed the hand-off share, which we call the hand-off ceiling: no backend can execute request that was never sent. Learning to act may also affect conversation: one policy decides (mt, wt) and at, so training it to act can change its conversational control (iv) and, because its speech is voiced from its internal states, the intelligibility of that speech. Duopra (Section 4) implements this policy with domain tools and query in the same action space, and Section 5 evaluates its task success together with these conversational and speech effects.

sections.title: 4 Duopra
sections.content: Duopra is full-duplex interaction model built on RV-Audio (Venus Team (Ant Group), Tsinghua University, 2026). It replaces the base models private free-text delegation requests with structured JSON actions. Figure 2 outlines the three training stages.

sections.title: 4.1 Unified Action Space
sections.content: Duopra retains the base models streaming loop. In each 1-s unit, the language model, or thinker, generates duplex control tokens and public text wt. The <listen> and <speak> tokens represent the turn state mt in Eq. (1). The speech generator, or talker, voices the text conditioned on the thinkers hidden states (Xu et al., 2025). To act within the same stream, Duopra encodes at in Eq. (1) as JSON in the thinkers private <delegate> span. Duopra uses select action to retrieve tool schemas and call action to invoke an exposed tool. The runtime validates each call and inserts its result as <backend> observation at the first unit boundary after the result returns. The backend is one more tool: Duopra delegates through the same call operation by invoking query. It supplies natural-language task description that contains the users latest values, requested steps, and dependencies. Appendix specifies the training and evaluation interfaces. 4 Figure 2: Duopras three training stages on RV-Audio (hj: thinker hidden state at spoken-token position j; Pϕ0 , Pϕ: base and Stage-3 projectors; cj: talker conditioning). Stage 1 trains the thinker on unit-level sessions and yields Duopra-SFT  (Table 5)  . Stage 2 trains thinker LoRA with Dr. GRPO in the sandbox of Section 4.3; Stage 2a yields Duopra-RL1 and Stage 2b yields Duopra-RL. Stage 3 freezes the Duopra-RL thinker and trains only its projector, producing the final Duopra model.

sections.title: 5.2 Main Results (RQ1)
sections.content: Both execution routes succeed. Table 1 summarizes all results. Duopra improves over both frontendbackend baselines whether it calls do7 main tools itself (Direct) or delegates through query (Backend). With the backend fixed to Qwen3-8B, replacing the frontend of RV-Audio + Harness with Duopra raises Pass@1 from 4.7% to 44.7%, and the paired 95% interval of this gain excludes zero (Table 13b). Without any inferencetime backend, Duopra performs comparably to its delegated configurations, so the trained frontend both executes tasks natively and supplies executable requests to frozen backend. Published reference points. Published results come from other evaluation setups and judges, so they provide context rather than ranking. In this context, Duopra performs on par with Gemini Live 2.5 and remains behind GPT-Realtime and Gemini Live 3.1 (Table 1a,b). Native execution under Both. When domain tools and query are both visible, Duopra performs similarly to Direct and almost never delegates; nearly all of its successes come from its own domain calls (Appendix F). Its task agency thus resides in the frontend and does not depend on calling the backend when the required tools are visible. 5. Initiation vs. Execution (RQ2) Having established that frontend can acquire task agency, we locate where some baselines lose it. Following Section 3, Pass@1 factors into call coverage (Call), the share of sessions with an executed domain-tool call, and conditional success (Passcall) among those sessions (Table 1; Figure 4). hand-off to query need not produce domain-tool call. Initiation limits the baseline. RV-Audio + Harness hands off in only 11.0% of sessions, so even perfect backend execution could not lift its Pass@1 above this hand-off ceiling. With the same backend, it differs from Duopra far more in Call than in Passcall  (Table 1)  . Where the gain comes from. Matched sessions locate the gain (Appendix F). On the few sessions in which RV-Audio + Harness executes domain call, Duopra is no more successful than the baseline. Its gain comes from the remaining sessions, which the baseline never executes and nearly half of which Duopra passes. Duopra thus improves Pass@1 by initiating requests that previously went unserved. Restricting the frontend to query costs both accuracy and time: with Qwen3-8B, Backend yields significantly more wrong-argument sessions than Both, and with either backend LLM it delays the factual answer (Table 13b; Appendix F.1). These outcomes reflect both the frontends request formulation and the backends execution. Effect of the backend. With Duopra fixed, replacing Qwen3-8B by DeepSeek raises conditional success but lowers call coverage, and the resulting change in Pass@1 is not significant (Table 13b). stronger backend improves the execution of initiated requests but cannot supply the requests themselves. In frontendbackend agents, task success is therefore limited first by initiation: execution can be offloaded, but initiating faithful request remains frontend responsibility.

sections.title: 5.4 From Initiation to Completion (RQ3)
sections.content: Since the bottleneck lies in initiation, we next examine how training removes it and which failures remain. From calls to completions. Stage 2a makes the policy call tools more often, yet its Pass@1 barely changes (Figure 3a): calling more is not completing more. Duopra then improves significantly over Duopra-RL1 (Table 13b), with the largest gains on 8 multi-call requests, which Duopra-RL1 never completes (Figure 3b). The share of sessions whose executed tool names and counts match the gold calls rises accordingly. Training thus first increases initiation and then converts it into complete execution. Residual errors. As no-call sessions decline, sessions with the correct tools but wrong argument become the largest failure class (Figure 3a). Selecting the required tools and preserving the users values are separate requirements for faithful execution. Table 16 illustrates both: corrected request executed correctly, and an order ID in which the letter becomes zero.

sections.title: 5.5 Conversation and Speech (RQ4)
sections.content: Task agency must not come at the expense of the conversational agency that makes the model fullduplex, or of the intelligibility of its speech. Turn-taking control. Duopra improves on RVAudio in all three FDB v1.0 takeover rates: it takes the turn more often when the user finishes or interrupts, and less often during pauses  (Table 1)  . The retention is behavior-specific rather than uniform, however: Duopra responds to fewer interruptions than Duopra-RL1, and none of the post-trained checkpoints produces backchannels on the tested items (Appendix F). Projector repair. With the Duopra-RL thinker held fixed, replacing the base projector with the Stage-3 projector more than halves Chinese CER and lowers English WER on the projectorselection set  (Table 15)  , and it moves the talker conditioning back toward that of RV-Audio (Figure 5). Task agency can thus coexist with key conversational agency in one causal policy, although spontaneous backchanneling remains to be recovered.

sections.title: 6 Conclusion
sections.content: This work examines how full-duplex interaction model can move from managing conversation to carrying out tasks. Our analysis answers both parts of the question posed in Section 1. In frontendbackend agents, task success is limited first by initiation: execution can be offloaded, but initiating faithful request remains frontend responsibility. We introduce Duopra, which learns to act through unified interface for domain-tool calls and natural-language backend requests. On FDB v3, Duopra recovers tasks left unexecuted by the evaluated baselines and improves multi-call completion beyond what more frequent invocation alone would explain. The resulting task agency coexists with improved performance on all three FDB v1.0 takeover rates, while projectoronly repair mitigates speech degradation. The loss of spontaneous backchanneling nevertheless shows that maintaining all conversational behaviors remains an open challenge.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.content: Comparability of published results. We include published results for commercial systems and several open-source baselines as reference points. Differences in evaluation setups, judges and scoring protocols limit direct comparisons with our own results. Model and data coverage. Duopra is built on single full-duplex interaction model and posttrained on synthetic speech from limited set of voices. Further evaluation is needed to determine whether the gains extend to other base models and more diverse speech conditions. Future work. Our tool-use evaluation on FDB v3 uses prerecorded user requests and simulated APIs. The fixed user input does not capture followup requests that arise from the agents responses or tool results. Future work could therefore evaluate Duopra in multi-turn tool-use tasks, assessing its ability to maintain task state and adapt subsequent actions as users clarify or revise their goals.

sections.content: Table 2 summarizes the model configuration and the training settings for all three stages. A.1 Base Model Duopra builds on the 9B RV-Audio model (Section 4). Its thinker controls the duplex stream with <listen>, <speak>, <chunk_eos> and <turn_eos>. The trainable and frozen components are listed in Table 2. The cross-entropy loss gives equal weight to public text, private actions and duplex control tokens, averaging first over target tokens within session and then over sessions. sections.title: D Reward Specification
sections.content: Table 7 lists the reward components used in Eq. (3). Table 8 gives the instructions for the reward judge. D.1 Scoring Evidence The scorer combines runtime checks with semantic labels from Qwen3.8-27B (Qwen Team, 2026). Runtime logs and the unit timeline establish action validity, executed tools and arguments, repeated calls, and the timing of speech and actions. Argument grounding is checked against the users latest stated values, earlier tool results and session context. The LLM judge evaluates claims in the public response using the observations available when those claims were made. Its inputs include the public text, observations permitted for each requested goal, and catalog of numeric result fields; its instruction is reproduced in Table 8. The judge returns structured labels for covered goals, fabricated results, false refusals, false claims of completion and spoken private metadata. Each covered goal requires proof containing the goal index, observation index, evidence type (result or observed failure) and verbatim quote. The output also identifies disclosures of unfinished steps and links stated result numbers, dates, times and identifiers to their supporting evidence fields. The accompanying reason is limited to twelve words. The scorer validates the output schema, verifies that quotes occur in the public text, and checks that each cited observation supports the specified goal and precedes the statement. It then parses the quoted numeric values and compares them with the cited fields after normalizing Chinese and Arabic numerals, spoken digit sequences, time expressions and full-width characters. For example, three nine five can mean 395, and six twelve can express the clock component of 18:12. Validated labels determine result-readout credit, fabrication and completion status; the deterministic outcome mapping then assigns the scalar reward. Invalid judgments leave rollout unscored and invoke the group-filtering procedure in Appendix A. The remaining reward components follow runtime rules, with semantic judgments used for value normalization and for distinguishing continued content from new response after interruption. D.2 Outcome Tiers For Stage-2a task families, RA sums the applicable components in Table 7, with clipping to [1, 1.2] and any applicable family-specific caps. For the five new Stage-2b task families, RB uses the outcome scores in Section 4.3. When call is required and none is executed, the score is 0.85 if the policy speaks and 0.90 if it stays silent. D.3 Timing and Backend Responsibility Timing rewards use 1-s units on the input-audio timeline. Interruption, cancellation and correction deadlines start at the onset of the corresponding user utterance; response and action deadlines start at the end of the request. The acting and stopping deadlines are kact = 3 and kstop = 2 units, respectively (Section 3). The control reward penalizes both delayed stops after interruptions and unnecessary stops after backchannels or background

ECAPA cosine: similarity to the native voice. 2023), interleaved reasoning and acting (Yao et al., 2023), and instruction tuning (Qin et al., 2024). BFCL (Patil et al., 2025) and τ -bench (Yao et al., 2025a) evaluate function calls and interactive task completion. GRPO retains PPOs clipped objective (Schulman et al., 2017) while replacing its value model with group-relative advantages (Shao et al., 2024). Dr. GRPO removes responselength and reward-standard-deviation normalizations (Liu et al., 2025); DAPO uses dynamic sampling to exclude groups with identical rewards (Yu et al., 2025a). Duopra applies this optimization framework to streaming sessions, with rewards for timely action, grounded arguments and task completion. Spoken agents and evaluation. Alongside FDB v3 (Lin et al., 2026a), benchmarks assess spoken tool calls (Jain et al., 2025; Pahwa et al., 2026) and end-to-end voice-agent performance (Ray et al., 2026; Bogavelli et al., 2026). Related systems delegate reasoning and tool use to background models (Thinking Machines Lab, 2026; Orantqing et al., 2026) or retrieve knowledge asynchronously (Chien et al., 2026). Our analysis separates frontend action initiation from subsequent tool execution using the resulting call traces. Sufficiency and dialogue state. Information sufficiency connects our setting to slot filling in schema-guided dialogue (Rastogi et al., 2020) and missing-information tests for tool use (Patil et al., 2025; Lu et al., 2025). Our formulation (Section 3) tracks the latest spoken values and corrections; delegated requests must also carry required dependencies. The same sufficiency rule applies to both routes.
